currentContext.expansion: The Haldia facility (acquired via the NCLT process) moved from acquisition to activation during FY 2025-26: a 33,000 MT tank farm and tin manufacturing/tin-filling/pouch-filling lines with cumulative capacity of 300 MT per day became operational, serving Odisha, West Bengal and the North East. Separately, the Company is taking steps to install a solar power plant to replace conventionally-sourced energy.

risks.risk: Raw material and input cost volatility
risks.note: Volatility in paddy, edible oilseed and crude edible oil prices, along with movements in fuel, packaging and freight costs, can affect input cost structures and margin stability in a highly competitive, price-sensitive consumer market.

risks.risk: High import dependence in edible oil
risks.note: Approximately 60% of India's edible oil requirement is sourced from abroad; disruption in palm oil supply from Malaysia/Indonesia, a poor soybean harvest in Argentina, or adverse weather affecting sunflower production in Ukraine/Russia can sharply raise landed costs and compress refining margins — already evidenced in FY26 when crude sunflower oil import costs hit Rs.114/kg in September 2025 and refined sunflower oil reached Rs.170-175/litre at retail in early 2026.

Sudden changes in import duties, export restrictions, stock limits, minimum support prices or procurement/food-subsidy policies can materially alter market access, cost structures, inventory valuations and margins over short periods; export restrictions on rice and higher edible-oil import duty already compressed FY26 standalone economics.

risks.risk: Intense competition from organised and unorganised players
risks.note: The Company competes with local millers, regional brands, large national players and unorganised suppliers in both rice and edible oils; price-led competition in value-conscious markets can restrict the ability to pass on input cost increases and pressure operating margins.

risks.risk: Dependence on rural incomes, crop output and monsoon behaviour
risks.note: Performance is closely linked to rural incomes, crop output, procurement policies and overall consumption sentiment; economic slowdown or adverse monsoon behaviour can impact demand and raw material availability across key product segments.
When palm oil becomes expensive relative to soybean oil, the entire import basket shifts, affecting procurement planning, storage decisions and refining operations simultaneously.

Rising expectations around food safety, traceability, packaging quality and sustainability standards require continuous investment in processes, technology and compliance; failure to keep pace with evolving consumer or regulatory requirements (fortification, labelling, traceability, sustainable sourcing) could weaken competitive positioning over time.

business_model.title: What they do
business_model.body: Halder Venture Limited is engaged in the manufacturing and sale of rice and edible oil as its principal businesses, with edible oil contributing approximately 73.88% of total standalone revenue. The Company also produces de-oiled rice bran as a by-product and has entered the branded aquaculture feed space, selling branded rice, edible oil and feed products to dealers, distributors and consumers across Eastern and North-Eastern India as well as select international markets.

demand_drivers.title: Demand & outlook drivers
demand_drivers.body:
- Export restrictions on rice and higher import duty on edible oil constrained standalone volumes and flexibility during FY 2025-26, particularly in the first half of the year; management expects to restore momentum in standalone earnings as these policy headwinds normalise
- Consolidated performance is being strengthened by Haldia's activation, branded growth and business diversification, offsetting standalone-level policy shocks and validating the strategic choice to diversify and integrate across product lines and markets
- Management intends to increase the share of volumes sold under own brands so that more of the topline is anchored in products that can command better margin and stronger customer loyalty
- Bringing Haldia's refinery into full operation is expected to make the combined storage, refining and packing complex a consistent contributor to revenue and profitability

capital_allocation.title: Strategy & capital allocation
capital_allocation.body:
- Build an integrated edible-oil platform centred around the Haldia facility, moving up the value chain from bulk trade to sourcing, refining, storage, packing and branded distribution
- Grow branded presence in rice, edible oils and value-added products across Eastern and North-Eastern India
- Deepen farmer relationships and progressively build traceability and sustainability into the value chain through a phased, staged partnership with agri-technology enterprise InQube
- Strengthen position in both domestic and export markets with a disciplined, brand-led approach
- Diversify and integrate across rice, edible oils, by-products and allied initiatives rather than remain dependent on a single line of business or a single set of markets
- Maintain a conservative approach to leverage, linking every borrowing to clear, measurable returns
- Strengthen risk management and governance processes, including implementation of an enhanced enterprise risk-management framework, in anticipation of a larger, more complex organisation

capex_expansion.title: Capex & expansion plans
capex_expansion.body: The Haldia facility (acquired via the NCLT process) moved from acquisition to activation during FY 2025-26: a 33,000 MT tank farm and tin manufacturing/tin-filling/pouch-filling lines with cumulative capacity of 300 MT per day became operational, serving Odisha, West Bengal and the North East. A planned 500 MT refinery at Haldia is expected to be commissioned in the final quarter of FY 2026-27, deepening backward integration into refining. At the Ahmadpur (Birbhum, West Bengal) rice manufacturing units, Unit I underwent engineering optimisation — integrating a dedicated steam line connecting existing and newer plant sections, improving boiler utilisation and cutting husk consumption/thermal losses (achieving steam savings of 24 tonnes/day) without significant capital expenditure — while Unit II underwent technological modernisation, replacing older milling equipment and raising milling capacity from 4 tonnes/hour to 6 tonnes/hour (a 50% increase), along with upgraded cleaning, grading and separation equipment. Separately, the Company is taking steps to install a solar power plant to replace conventionally-sourced energy.

moat.title: Bull — competitive strengths
moat.body:
- Century-long (100-year) legacy relationships directly with paddy-farming families in Ahmadpur, Bengal, spanning generations
- Trusted brand positioning in daily-necessity, non-discretionary categories (rice and edible oil) supporting the shift from unbranded to branded consumption
- Direct-from-farmer paddy sourcing (bypassing aggregators) giving access to niche paddy varieties not reliably available through intermediaries, supporting a differentiated branded rice portfolio
- Newly activated integrated Haldia facility (tank farm, tin/pouch filling, upcoming refinery) deepening backward integration in edible oil
- Expanding multi-state distribution network across Bihar, Jharkhand, West Bengal and the North East, with separate dedicated networks for rice, edible oil and de-oiled rice bran
- International market presence and visibility via trade shows (Gulfood Dubai, PRODEXPO Moscow, Ivory Coast Food Expo, Bengal Aquaculture Expo) across Russia, West Africa, Bangladesh and Vietnam

risks.title: Bear — key risks
risks.body:
- Raw material and input cost volatility — Volatility in paddy, edible oilseed and crude edible oil prices, along with movements in fuel, packaging and freight costs, can affect input cost structures and margin stability in a highly competitive, price-sensitive consumer market.
- High import dependence in edible oil — Approximately 60% of India's edible oil requirement is sourced from abroad; disruption in palm oil supply from Malaysia/Indonesia, a poor soybean harvest in Argentina, or adverse weather affecting sunflower production in Ukraine/Russia can sharply raise landed costs and compress refining margins — already evidenced in FY26 when crude sunflower oil import costs hit Rs.114/kg in September 2025 and refined sunflower oil reached Rs.170-175/litre at retail in early 2026.
- Policy and regulatory sensitivity — Sudden changes in import duties, export restrictions, stock limits, minimum support prices or procurement/food-subsidy policies can materially alter market access, cost structures, inventory valuations and margins over short periods; export restrictions on rice and higher edible-oil import duty already compressed FY26 standalone economics.
- Intense competition from organised and unorganised players — The Company competes with local millers, regional brands, large national players and unorganised suppliers in both rice and edible oils; price-led competition in value-conscious markets can restrict the ability to pass on input cost increases and pressure operating margins.
- Dependence on rural incomes, crop output and monsoon behaviour — Performance is closely linked to rural incomes, crop output, procurement policies and overall consumption sentiment; economic slowdown or adverse monsoon behaviour can impact demand and raw material availability across key product segments.
- Inter-oil price differential exposure — When palm oil becomes expensive relative to soybean oil, the entire import basket shifts, affecting procurement planning, storage decisions and refining operations simultaneously.
- Rising compliance and quality-standard expectations — Rising expectations around food safety, traceability, packaging quality and sustainability standards require continuous investment in processes, technology and compliance; failure to keep pace with evolving consumer or regulatory requirements (fortification, labelling, traceability, sustainable sourcing) could weaken competitive positioning over time.
